subject: Moving a 300-person customer support organisation to a four-day, 32-hour week from Q2, judged against the four attached sources (Kestrel blog, Nordvik et al. 2026 cluster-RCT working paper, Workforce Pulse 2025 vendor survey, Varmland municipal trial)
decisionObjective: Decide, ahead of the leadership offsite, whether to roll out a 32-hour four-day week across all 300 support staff from Q2, run a limited and measured pilot first (for example with staggered schedules), or not proceed. The decision should rest on what credible evidence shows about objective productivity, service levels such as first-response time and coverage, wellbeing and retention for support work specifically. It should not rest on the COO's claim of a 40% productivity gain, which is treated here as a premise to test.

criteria.name: Strength and relevance of the evidence for each claimed effect
criteria.rationale: The four sources range from a randomised trial with objective outcomes down to self-reports with no control group and a hypothetical vendor poll. How much each finding can be trusted, and how well it transfers to a support org, decides how much weight it gets in the recommendation.

criteria.name: Objective output and throughput per team (tickets resolved, output per paid hour)
criteria.rationale: The COO's case rests on productivity. Support output can be counted in tickets resolved, so the decision should turn on objective throughput, not self-rated productivity. The question is whether a 20% cut in hours is offset.

criteria.name: Service levels and coverage (first-response time, SLA attainment, cover during operating hours)
criteria.rationale: Support is a coverage-bound function. Nordvik reports first-response time 11% slower for service teams unless schedules are staggered. Customer-facing service levels are the main operational risk specific to this org.

criteria.name: Employee wellbeing and burnout
criteria.rationale: Burnout is a known problem in support. A validated improvement (0.4 SD in Nordvik) is a real benefit to weigh against service and cost risk.

criteria.name: Voluntary attrition and the replacement costs it avoids
criteria.rationale: Support orgs usually have high turnover and high hiring and training costs. The attrition difference (9.1% vs 13.0%) could fund some of any coverage gap, so retention bears directly on the business case.

criteria.name: Cost and implementation feasibility (overtime, extra headcount, scheduling design, Q2 timeline)
criteria.rationale: Varmland saw overtime costs rise 6%, and staggered rostering is needed to protect response times. Whether a Q2 company-wide launch can be done without hidden cost or SLA damage decides between full rollout and a pilot.

assumptionsToVerify.assumption: 'The research is clear: a four-day week raises productivity by 40%'
assumptionsToVerify.howToCheck: Trace the 40% to its source (likely Kestrel's self-rated survey) and compare it with objective controlled evidence (Nordvik: -2% team output, 95% CI -7% to +3%). Check whether any rigorous study supports a 40% gain in total output.

assumptionsToVerify.assumption: The evidence is 'clear' and applies uniformly across job types, including customer support
assumptionsToVerify.howToCheck: Compare the support subgroup results in Nordvik (first-response time +11% unless staggered) with the overall results, and note that Kestrel covers engineering and design staff while Varmland is a municipal trial with a different hours change.

assumptionsToVerify.assumption: A company-wide switch from Q2 is feasible without degrading service
assumptionsToVerify.howToCheck: Check the org's coverage needs and SLA headroom (internal data) against Nordvik's staggered-schedule finding and Varmland's overtime increase.

assumptionsToVerify.assumption: The source summaries in sources/ accurately reflect the underlying studies (for example, the Nordvik working paper exists and reports these figures)
assumptionsToVerify.howToCheck: Where possible, find the original Nordvik, Achebe & Lund (2026) working paper and the Varmland public report and check the figures, confidence intervals and methods. Flag anything that cannot be verified.

assumptionsToVerify.assumption: The 9-month Nordvik effects (wellbeing, attrition) last beyond the trial period and are not novelty or Hawthorne effects
assumptionsToVerify.howToCheck: Look for follow-up data in Nordvik or in other long-running four-day-week trials on whether the effects fade over time, and note that this remains uncertain if no such data exist.

evidenceByGap.question: Is there any credible, controlled, objectively measured evidence of a productivity gain near 40% from a four-day or 32-hour week, and where does the COO's figure come from (it appears to match Kestrel's self-rated 40%)?

evidence.claim: Kestrel Software (company blog, 2025): single company, 60 employees (engineering and design); productivity measured by an employee self-assessment survey before and after the switch; no comparison group; '40% average increase in self-rated productivity'.
evidence.applicability: This is the most likely origin of the COO's '40%' figure, since the number and wording match. It does not transfer well to a 300-person support org: different work type, self-rated outcome, n=60, no control.
evidence.limitations: The 40% is self-rated productivity, not objective output. There is no control group, it is a company marketing blog, and it has selection and expectancy bias. We do not know how long after the switch the survey was run. Pay terms are not stated (see E19).

evidence.claim: Nordvik, Achebe & Lund (2026) working paper: cluster-randomised trial of 112 teams in 9 firms (including 31 customer-service teams), randomised to a 32-hour week vs control for 9 months. Output per team (objective: tickets resolved, billable output) -2% (95% CI -7% to +3%).
evidence.applicability: This is the strongest design among the sources (randomised, objective output) and it includes support-like work. Its central estimate is roughly flat total output, which is incompatible with a 40% gain in total output.
evidence.limitations: It is a working paper, and peer-review and pre-registration status are not stated. The fixture is a short summary only. It does not give baseline hours, pay terms, the subgroup output result for customer-service teams, attrition or contamination checks, or how 'output' was aggregated across firms. We could not find the paper externally (see E8).

evidence.claim: Microsoft Japan's 2019 'Work Life Choice Challenge' (offices closed every Friday in August 2019) was widely reported as boosting productivity by about 40%. That figure is sales per employee in August 2019 vs August 2018, and it was a year-on-year comparison with no control group.
evidence.applicability: This is the other well-known public source of a '40%' four-day-week figure, and could be what the COO means. It is a one-month, uncontrolled, sales-per-employee proxy at a sales and software subsidiary, so it is not evidence about total support throughput.
evidence.limitations: In the first round only the headline '~40%' was corroborated across outlets' titles. The measurement details are now addressed by E22 (a second, independent search). The NPR fetch failed (host not allowed).

evidence.claim: The COO states 'the research is clear: a four-day week raises productivity by 40%'. The organisation is a 300-person customer support org, and the proposal is a four-day, 32-hour week from Q2.
evidence.applicability: This is the premise to test. The 40% matches Kestrel's self-rated figure (E1) and the Microsoft Japan sales-per-employee headline (E10, E22). Neither is a controlled measure of total output.
evidence.limitations: It is a user-reported claim and the COO's actual source is unknown. The request does not say whether the 32-hour week would keep full pay or cut pay pro rata.

evidence.claim: Microsoft Japan 'Work-Life Choice Challenge Summer 2019': about 2,300 employees were given every Friday off in August 2019. Multiple outlets report a 39.9% rise in sales per employee compared with August 2018 ('labor productivity increased by 39.9% compared with August 2018, the company said'), drawn from a Microsoft Japan report. Other reported results: printing down 58.7%, and 92.1% of employees said they liked the four-day week. Meetings were limited to 30 minutes.
evidence.applicability: Addresses D7. It confirms that the ~40% is sales per employee for one month, compared year on year (August 2019 vs August 2018). It is a company-reported revenue ratio, not a measure of output or throughput.
evidence.limitations: No page was inspected (weforum.org fetch failed; NPR failed in round 1). This is a second synthesized search summary that agrees with the first-round summary behind E10, so the measurement detail now rests on two searches attributing it to several outlets. 'No control group' is an inference from the year-on-year design: no source describes a comparison group. A YoY sales comparison is confounded by seasonality, product cycles and the shorter month of working days.

evidence.claim: Microsoft Japan pay terms: sources differ slightly. One says full-time employees got paid leave (special paid leave) on the closure Fridays. Another, citing Mainichi, says all employees got five Fridays off in August 'without any reduction in salary and annual leave'. Neither version describes a pay cut.
evidence.applicability: Addresses D1. The Microsoft Japan result came under full pay, so it says nothing about a pro-rata design.
evidence.limitations: From a single search summary that does not tie each pay statement to a specific URL. Not fetched.

evidenceByGap.question: What exactly do Nordvik et al. report for the 31 customer-service teams? This covers output, first-response time with and without staggered schedules, attrition and wellbeing within the subgroup, how staggering was implemented, and whether the working paper is peer-reviewed, pre-registered and free of attrition or contamination problems.

evidence.claim: Nordvik, Achebe & Lund (2026) working paper: cluster-randomised trial of 112 teams in 9 firms (including 31 customer-service teams), randomised to a 32-hour week vs control for 9 months. Output per team (objective: tickets resolved, billable output) -2% (95% CI -7% to +3%).
evidence.applicability: This is the strongest design among the sources (randomised, objective output) and it includes support-like work. Its central estimate is roughly flat total output, which is incompatible with a 40% gain in total output.
evidence.limitations: It is a working paper, and peer-review and pre-registration status are not stated. The fixture is a short summary only. It does not give baseline hours, pay terms, the subgroup output result for customer-service teams, attrition or contamination checks, or how 'output' was aggregated across firms. We could not find the paper externally (see E8).

evidence.claim: Nordvik et al. customer-service teams subgroup: first-response time +11% slower (95% CI +4% to +18%) unless staggered schedules were used.
evidence.applicability: This is directly relevant to a support org. It points to a real service-level risk if everyone takes the same day off, and suggests staggering as a mitigation.
evidence.limitations: The fixture does not report the effect size with staggering, how many of the 31 teams staggered, whether staggering was randomised or self-selected, how staggering was implemented, or subgroup output, attrition and wellbeing. 'Unless staggered' may hide confounding.

evidence.claim: Nordvik et al.: wellbeing (validated burnout scale) improved by 0.4 SD; voluntary attrition 9.1% vs 13.0% annualised.
evidence.applicability: These are relevant to support burnout and turnover costs. Whether the attrition gap matters financially depends on the org's own baseline turnover and cost per hire (G5).
evidence.limitations: No CI is given for either the wellbeing or the attrition result. 9.1% is presumably the treatment arm and 13.0% the control, but the fixture does not label them. The figures are pooled, not support-specific. Nine months is short for annualised attrition, and novelty effects cannot be ruled out from this source. See E18 for the between-arm vs within-arm ambiguity and the absence of pay terms.

evidence.claim: A web search found no trace of a 2026 working paper by Nordvik, Achebe and Lund on a four-day-week cluster-randomised trial. The existence of the paper, its peer-review and pre-registration status, and its reported figures could not be independently checked.
evidence.ref: WebSearch: Nordvik Achebe Lund 2026 working paper four-day week cluster-randomised trial
evidence.applicability: The key source's figures rest only on the supplied summary, so the synthesis should flag this provenance caveat.
evidence.limitations: Not being found by one search does not prove the paper doesn't exist. It may be unpublished, unindexed or circulated internally.

evidence.claim: Re-read of source-B (Nordvik): the summary says nothing about pay terms for the 32-hour arm (full pay or pro rata). The wellbeing line reads only 'Wellbeing (validated burnout scale): improved by 0.4 SD'. It does not say whether this is a treatment-vs-control difference or a before-and-after change within the treatment arm, and it gives no CI, p-value or significance test. The attrition line reads only 'Voluntary attrition: 9.1% vs 13.0% annualised', with no arm labels, no CI, no p-value and no significance test. The only CIs in the summary are for team output (-7% to +3%) and customer-service first-response time (+4% to +18%).
evidence.applicability: Addresses D1 and D2. Without pay terms, we cannot say whether the wellbeing and attrition effects would carry over under either pay design. Without a between-arm label and some measure of uncertainty, the 0.4 SD and the 3.9-point attrition gap are point estimates of unknown significance. 'Validated' describes the burnout scale, not the finding.
evidence.limitations: This is a statement about what the supplied summary contains and omits. The underlying paper may report these details, but it could not be located (E8).

evidenceByGap.question: Recomputed from the sources: what output per paid hour does Nordvik imply (0.98/0.80 = about +22.5% per hour, but about -2% total output), what is the relative attrition reduction ((13.0-9.1)/13.0 = about 30%), and how do these numbers differ from the claimed '40% productivity'?

evidence.claim: Nordvik et al.: wellbeing (validated burnout scale) improved by 0.4 SD; voluntary attrition 9.1% vs 13.0% annualised.
evidence.applicability: These are relevant to support burnout and turnover costs. Whether the attrition gap matters financially depends on the org's own baseline turnover and cost per hire (G5).
evidence.limitations: No CI is given for either the wellbeing or the attrition result. 9.1% is presumably the treatment arm and 13.0% the control, but the fixture does not label them. The figures are pooled, not support-specific. Nine months is short for annualised attrition, and novelty effects cannot be ruled out from this source. See E18 for the between-arm vs within-arm ambiguity and the absence of pay terms.

evidence.claim: Arithmetic implied by the Nordvik figures: if hours were cut 40->32 (a 20% cut), total output of 0.98 implies output per paid hour of about 0.98/0.80 = 1.225 (+22.5%), while total output is about -2%. The attrition difference 13.0 - 9.1 = 3.9 percentage points is a relative reduction of 3.9/13.0 = 30%. Neither figure equals a '40% productivity' gain in total output.
evidence.applicability: Gives the offsite defensible numbers and separates per-hour from total output, and relative from absolute attrition.
evidence.limitations: Nordvik's baseline hours are not stated, so the 20% cut is an assumption. Using the CI bounds (-7% to +3%), per-hour change would range from about +16% to +29%. The per-hour gain does not add capacity: a support org handles total demand, so total output is the operative metric. Downstream stages should recheck this arithmetic.

evidence.claim: Re-read of source-B (Nordvik): the summary says nothing about pay terms for the 32-hour arm (full pay or pro rata). The wellbeing line reads only 'Wellbeing (validated burnout scale): improved by 0.4 SD'. It does not say whether this is a treatment-vs-control difference or a before-and-after change within the treatment arm, and it gives no CI, p-value or significance test. The attrition line reads only 'Voluntary attrition: 9.1% vs 13.0% annualised', with no arm labels, no CI, no p-value and no significance test. The only CIs in the summary are for team output (-7% to +3%) and customer-service first-response time (+4% to +18%).
evidence.applicability: Addresses D1 and D2. Without pay terms, we cannot say whether the wellbeing and attrition effects would carry over under either pay design. Without a between-arm label and some measure of uncertainty, the 0.4 SD and the 3.9-point attrition gap are point estimates of unknown significance. 'Validated' describes the burnout scale, not the finding.
evidence.limitations: This is a statement about what the supplied summary contains and omits. The underlying paper may report these details, but it could not be located (E8).

evidenceByGap.question: How well do Kestrel (60 engineering and design staff, self-report, no control), Workforce Pulse (hypothetical 'would be more productive', vendor-run) and Varmland (36 hours rather than four days, municipal, management-assessed 'maintained' service) transfer to a 300-person support org, and what does each validly show?

evidence.claim: Kestrel Software (company blog, 2025): single company, 60 employees (engineering and design); productivity measured by an employee self-assessment survey before and after the switch; no comparison group; '40% average increase in self-rated productivity'.
evidence.applicability: This is the most likely origin of the COO's '40%' figure, since the number and wording match. It does not transfer well to a 300-person support org: different work type, self-rated outcome, n=60, no control.
evidence.limitations: The 40% is self-rated productivity, not objective output. There is no control group, it is a company marketing blog, and it has selection and expectancy bias. We do not know how long after the switch the survey was run. Pay terms are not stated (see E19).

evidence.claim: Workforce Pulse Survey 2025 (HR software vendor): 71% of 4,000 respondents say they *would* be more productive on a 4-day week.
evidence.applicability: This measures employee appetite or attitude, not an effect. It is useful only as a signal of staff demand or recruitment appeal.
evidence.limitations: It is hypothetical, self-predicted and vendor-run, with sampling, sector mix and question wording unknown. It does not say whether respondents assumed full or reduced pay. It cannot support any productivity claim.

evidence.claim: Varmland municipal working-time trial (public report, 2024): weekly hours reduced from 40 to 36 (not four days). Service levels 'maintained' per management assessment; overtime costs rose 6%.
evidence.applicability: The +6% overtime cost is a relevant warning that coverage-bound services absorb shorter hours partly through paid overtime. The intervention was milder (a 10% cut, not 20%, and not a four-day pattern), so the cost for a 32-hour support week could be larger.
evidence.limitations: 'Maintained' service is a management judgement, not objective metrics. There is no control group, the setting is municipal, the baseline for the 6% is unspecified, pay terms are not stated (E19), and we could not find the report externally (see E9).

evidence.claim: A web search found no public report of a Varmland municipal 36-hour trial with a 6% overtime cost rise, so the figures could not be independently checked.
evidence.ref: WebSearch: Värmland municipal working time trial 36 hours report overtime costs
evidence.applicability: This is a provenance caveat for source D.
evidence.limitations: Only one English-language search was run. A Swedish-language search was not tried.

evidence.claim: Fan, Schor et al. (Nature Human Behaviour, July 2025): a six-month four-day-week, no-pay-cut trial of about 2,896 employees at 141 volunteer companies in six countries, compared with about 290 employees at 12 control companies. It reported reduced burnout and better job satisfaction and mental and physical health. Firms that cut about 8 hours per week saw the largest gains. Companies self-selected through 4 Day Week Global, so the study was not randomised.
evidence.applicability: This is independent support for the direction of Nordvik's wellbeing effect (E4), under no-pay-cut conditions. It does not address objective output or support-specific service levels.
evidence.limitations: Outcomes are self-reported. Firms are volunteers, mostly small and from English-speaking countries, and the control group is small. The SciAm fetch failed, so the details come from a search summary only. The 'no pay cut' term rests on this first-round summary alone; the follow-up search (E21) did not restate it. The control count here (~290) differs from E21 (285).

evidence.claim: UK 2022 four-day-week pilot one-year follow-up ('Making It Stick', Autonomy, Universities of Cambridge and Salford, February 2024): at least 54 of 61 organisations (89%) were still running the policy a year later, and 31 (51%) had made it permanent. Researchers reported that the wellbeing and burnout improvements were maintained at one year.
evidence.applicability: This is partial evidence that wellbeing effects are not purely novelty effects over about 12 months, which bears on the durability assumption.
evidence.limitations: Firms are self-selected and data are self-reported. Only part of the cohort joined the follow-up (one source says 28 organisations, another says employees from 47 companies). The sample is not sector-specific. The fetch of autonomy.work failed, so only the 89% and 51% retention figures are corroborated across domains. The wellbeing persistence comes from search summaries.

evidence.claim: UK 2022 pilot (original six-month results): organisations cut hours by an average of 6.6 to a 31.6-hour week, revenue rose marginally (+1.4% on average, company-reported), and 71% of employees reported less burnout. Customer-facing businesses such as call centres had service-level issues, and some needed to recruit additional headcount at extra cost. Staggered or set days off were the usual workaround. One contact centre noted that Monday and Friday peaks prevented days off on either side of the weekend.
evidence.applicability: This is directly relevant to the coverage and cost question (G6). It is consistent with Nordvik's finding that response time depends on staggering and with Varmland's overtime rise.
evidence.limitations: The call-centre service-level and extra-headcount points come from a single search summary, and which result each statement came from could not be confirmed. Revenue is company-reported, there is no sector breakdown, and no call-centre metrics (response times or SLA) were published.

evidence.claim: South Cambridgeshire District Council four-day-week trial (independent analysis by the Universities of Cambridge and Salford, 2024): 22 of 24 KPIs improved or stayed the same, and two worsened (for example, housing relet times went from 28 to 30 days). The percentage of contact-centre calls answered was reported among the improved measures. The council reported turnover down 39%.
evidence.applicability: This is one of the few cases with objective service KPIs that include contact-centre call answering. It suggests a contact operation can hold service levels with design effort.
evidence.limitations: The 22/24 figure appears in several outlets, but the call-answering detail and the 39% turnover figure come from the search summary. The turnover figure is from the council leader (an advocate). It is a public-sector case, not randomised, trial dates are reported inconsistently, and exact call figures were not accessed (the scambs.gov.uk fetch failed). A ministerial concern about fewer calls answered is recorded separately (E24). The scheduling design behind the result is undocumented (E25).

evidence.claim: Re-read of source-D (Varmland): the summary states only the 40-to-36 hour reduction, management-assessed 'maintained' service and the 6% overtime cost rise. It does not say whether pay was held at the 40-hour level or reduced pro rata. Source-A (Kestrel) and source-C (Workforce Pulse) are also silent on pay. None of the four supplied sources states the pay terms.
evidence.applicability: Addresses D1. The 6% overtime figure cannot be read as the full cost of the change, because the base pay cost (any wage held constant on fewer hours) is not stated. The supplied evidence gives no basis for assuming either full or reduced pay.
evidence.limitations: These records state omissions in the summaries. The original reports may contain pay terms.

evidence.claim: UK 2022 pilot (June to December 2022, 61 companies, over 2,900 workers) used the '100:80:100' model: 100% pay for 80% of the time, in exchange for maintaining 100% productivity. Firms chose their own design. Some used a condensed week, and others let staff choose their four days.
evidence.applicability: Addresses D1. The UK pilot's wellbeing, retention and revenue results (E12, E13) were obtained at full pay. They do not tell us what a pro-rata pay cut would produce, and under full pay the cost per paid hour rises. Letting firms choose the day pattern is relevant to staggering design.
evidence.limitations: Taken from a single synthesized search summary. The summary's own wording ('paid for 80% of their hours') is garbled relative to the standard 100:80:100 description, so the exact phrasing is unconfirmed. The WebFetch of weforum.org failed (ENOTFOUND). Other result titles (4dayweek.com, raconteur.net, personio.com) were returned but not inspected.

evidence.claim: Fan, Schor, Kelly and Gu (2025), 'Work time reduction via a 4-day workweek finds improvements in workers' well-being', is reported as published in Nature Human Behaviour. Sample: 2,896 employees across 141 organisations in six countries, compared with 285 employees at 12 control companies, over six months. Burnout fell from 2.83 to 2.38 on a 1-to-5 scale. Average working hours fell by about five hours per week. Participating companies volunteered, and the authors call for future randomised trials.
evidence.applicability: Addresses D7. The Nature Human Behaviour venue is reported consistently across two separate searches and several domains, including Nature's own Asia site. That supports calling it a journal publication rather than a working paper. The study is controlled but not randomised, and outcomes are self-reported.
evidence.limitations: No page was inspected: the theregister.com fetch failed (ENOTFOUND), as did SciAm in the first round. Peer review is inferred from the journal's standard review process, not confirmed from the article. The control count (285) differs from the first-round summary (~290, E11). The no-pay-cut term was not restated in this search, so it still rests on E11 alone. The reported mean hours reduction (~5 h/week) is smaller than the 8-hour cut proposed here.

evidence.claim: Microsoft Japan pay terms: sources differ slightly. One says full-time employees got paid leave (special paid leave) on the closure Fridays. Another, citing Mainichi, says all employees got five Fridays off in August 'without any reduction in salary and annual leave'. Neither version describes a pay cut.
evidence.applicability: Addresses D1. The Microsoft Japan result came under full pay, so it says nothing about a pro-rata design.
evidence.limitations: From a single search summary that does not tie each pay statement to a specific URL. Not fetched.

evidence.claim: South Cambridgeshire: the council's four-day-week pages say staff are expected to do 100% of their work in around 80% of their contracted hours, without reduction in pay. Full opening hours are maintained at no less than before, residents can contact the council on any day of the week, and the new patterns allowed a trial of early-evening opening one day a week (reported as Wednesdays). Staff 'use their scheduled rest day in a variety of ways'. Separately, a minister raised concerns about a reduction in the number of calls answered by the contact centre and the number resolved first time.
evidence.applicability: Addresses D1 and D5. The South Cambs result was obtained at full pay. Maintaining five-day opening while each person works four days requires rest days to be spread across the week in some form, but the specific contact-centre design is not described (E25). The ministerial concern conflicts with the 'calls answered improved' finding in E15, which may reflect a different metric (count vs percentage) or period.
evidence.limitations: From a single search summary. The scambs.gov.uk fetch failed in the first round and was not retried. The ministerial concern and the independent report's improvement may refer to different measures or periods, and this was not resolved.

evidenceByGap.question: What are this org's baseline figures: current first-response and resolution SLAs, operating hours and channel coverage needs, current voluntary attrition and cost per hire or ramp time, and whether demand is staffed to capacity?

evidence.claim: The org's baseline figures (current first-response and resolution SLAs and headroom, operating hours and channel coverage, voluntary attrition rate, cost per hire and ramp time, utilisation versus demand) are not in the sources or the request.
evidence.applicability: These figures are needed to turn the source effects (+11% first-response time without staggering, about 30% relative attrition reduction) into a cost/benefit case. The intended pay terms (full vs pro rata) are also internal and missing.
evidence.limitations: Only the user's internal data can fill this gap.

evidence.claim: Svartedalen elderly-care home, Gothenburg (6-hour day trial, ended February 2017): to cover reduced hours for about 68 nurses, the home hired about 17 extra staff at a reported cost of about 12 million kronor (about $1.3 million). Another report frames this as about a 25% staffing increase and about 6 million kronor per year. The city judged it too costly to make permanent, though partial offsets (for example, lower unemployment costs) were noted.
evidence.applicability: This is an analogue for a coverage-bound service: holding service constant under shorter hours required about 25% more headcount. That is a cost scenario the support org should model if staggering alone cannot protect SLAs.
evidence.limitations: The setting is elder care with 24/7 shifts, not support. The cost figures vary in framing across reports (total vs per year), and the corroboration rests on syndicated wire copy, so independence is limited.

evidence.claim: South Cambridgeshire District Council four-day-week trial (independent analysis by the Universities of Cambridge and Salford, 2024): 22 of 24 KPIs improved or stayed the same, and two worsened (for example, housing relet times went from 28 to 30 days). evidence.applicability: This is one of the few cases with objective service KPIs that include contact-centre call answering. It suggests a contact operation can hold service levels with design effort.
evidence.limitations: The 22/24 figure appears in several outlets, but the call-answering detail and the 39% turnover figure come from the search summary. The turnover figure is from the council leader (an advocate). It is a public-sector case, not randomised, trial dates are reported inconsistently, and exact call figures were not accessed (the scambs.gov.uk fetch failed). A ministerial concern about fewer calls answered is recorded separately (E24). The scheduling design behind the result is undocumented (E25).

evidence.claim: Re-read of source-D (Varmland): the summary states only the 40-to-36 hour reduction, management-assessed 'maintained' service and the 6% overtime cost rise. It does not say whether pay was held at the 40-hour level or reduced pro rata. Source-A (Kestrel) and source-C (Workforce Pulse) are also silent on pay. None of the four supplied sources states the pay terms.
evidence.applicability: Addresses D1. The 6% overtime figure cannot be read as the full cost of the change, because the base pay cost (any wage held constant on fewer hours) is not stated. The supplied evidence gives no basis for assuming either full or reduced pay.
evidence.limitations: These records state omissions in the summaries. The original reports may contain pay terms.

evidence.claim: UK 2022 pilot (June to December 2022, 61 companies, over 2,900 workers) used the '100:80:100' model: 100% pay for 80% of the time, in exchange for maintaining 100% productivity. Firms chose their own design. Some used a condensed week, and others let staff choose their four days.
evidence.applicability: Addresses D1. The UK pilot's wellbeing, retention and revenue results (E12, E13) were obtained at full pay. They do not tell us what a pro-rata pay cut would produce, and under full pay the cost per paid hour rises. Letting firms choose the day pattern is relevant to staggering design.
evidence.limitations: Taken from a single synthesized search summary. The summary's own wording ('paid for 80% of their hours') is garbled relative to the standard 100:80:100 description, so the exact phrasing is unconfirmed. The WebFetch of weforum.org failed (ENOTFOUND). Other result titles (4dayweek.com, raconteur.net, personio.com) were returned but not inspected.

evidence.claim: South Cambridgeshire: the council's four-day-week pages say staff are expected to do 100% of their work in around 80% of their contracted hours, without reduction in pay. Full opening hours are maintained at no less than before, residents can contact the council on any day of the week, and the new patterns allowed a trial of early-evening opening one day a week (reported as Wednesdays). Staff 'use their scheduled rest day in a variety of ways'. Separately, a minister raised concerns about a reduction in the number of calls answered by the contact centre and the number resolved first time.
evidence.applicability: Addresses D1 and D5. The South Cambs result was obtained at full pay. Maintaining five-day opening while each person works four days requires rest days to be spread across the week in some form, but the specific contact-centre design is not described (E25). The ministerial concern conflicts with the 'calls answered improved' finding in E15, which may reflect a different metric (count vs percentage) or period.
evidence.limitations: From a single search summary. The scambs.gov.uk fetch failed in the first round and was not retried. The ministerial concern and the independent report's improvement may refer to different measures or periods, and this was not resolved.

evidence.claim: No retrieved source states whether South Cambridgeshire's contact centre used staggered, rotating or rostered rest days. The draft's statement that South Cambs 'presumably used rostering design' has no direct support. The most the evidence allows (E24) is the inference that some spreading of rest days was needed to keep full five-day opening hours.
evidence.ref: WebSearch: South Cambridgeshire four-day week contact centre staggered rota cover five days
evidence.applicability: Addresses D5. The South Cambs vs Nordvik (E15 vs E3) contradiction should stay unresolved, or be labelled as speculation about scheduling design.
evidence.limitations: Only one targeted search was possible before the budget ran out. The search summary suggested the council's Cabinet papers (for example, the May 2023 results report at scambs.moderngov.co.uk) might give the rota design, but they were not inspected.

contradictions.aClaim: Fan, Schor et al. (Nature Human Behaviour, July 2025): a six-month four-day-week, no-pay-cut trial of about 2,896 employees at 141 volunteer companies in six countries, compared with about 290 employees at 12 control companies. It reported reduced burnout and better job satisfaction and mental and physical health. Firms that cut about 8 hours per week saw the largest gains. Companies self-selected through 4 Day Week Global, so the study was not randomised.
contradictions.bClaim: Fan, Schor, Kelly and Gu (2025), 'Work time reduction via a 4-day workweek finds improvements in workers' well-being', is reported as published in Nature Human Behaviour. Sample: 2,896 employees across 141 organisations in six countries, compared with 285 employees at 12 control companies, over six months. Burnout fell from 2.83 to 2.38 on a 1-to-5 scale. Average working hours fell by about five hours per week. Participating companies volunteered, and the authors call for future randomised trials.

unresolvedGaps.reason: We could not find or inspect the original Nordvik, Achebe & Lund (2026) working paper. Pay terms, peer-review and pre-registration status, whether the 0.4 SD wellbeing figure is between-arm, CIs or significance for wellbeing and attrition, arm labels, staggering implementation and the staggered-schedule effect size are all unknown beyond the fixture summary (E18).

The org's internal baselines (SLAs, coverage hours, attrition, cost per hire, utilisation) and its intended pay terms (full vs pro rata at 32 hours) were not supplied and cannot be researched externally.

No source describes the South Cambridgeshire contact-centre rota (E25). No published source gave objective response-time or SLA data for staggered versus non-staggered support schedules, or the overtime or headcount cost of staggering.

We could not find the Varmland public report to verify the 36-hour design, pay terms, the basis for 'maintained' service, or the 6% overtime figure. Pay terms for Fan, Schor et al. (no pay cut) rest on one first-round search summary (E11). The UK pilot's 100:80:100 terms rest on one summary (E20).

Which source the COO took the 40% from is unconfirmed. Candidates are Kestrel's self-rated figure and Microsoft Japan's 39.9% sales-per-employee YoY figure. No controlled study found shows a 40% gain in total output.
Durability beyond 9 months for Nordvik's effects is unknown. The only external durability evidence is the self-selected, self-reported UK pilot one-year follow-up.

Budget exhausted: WebSearch hit 13/12 for this run, so the planned searches on the Nature Human Behaviour DOI page and the South Cambs rota were denied. All WebFetch attempts failed with ENOTFOUND, because these hosts are outside the session's allowed network domains: www.npr.org, www.scientificamerican.com, autonomy.work, www.scambs.gov.uk, www.theregister.com, www.weforum.org and weforum.org. They would need to be allowed in the session's network settings. All web evidence rests on search results only, and no web page was directly inspected.
